html:
This map label marks the early speakers of Bantu languages in west central Africa, shown in 3000 and 2000 BCE, before their descendants spread across most of the southern half of the continent.

The Bantu languages are one branch of the large Niger-Congo family. By comparing the hundreds of Bantu languages spoken today, linguists place their homeland near the border of modern Nigeria and Cameroon. From there, in the Bantu expansion, speakers moved south through the rainforest and east toward the Great Lakes, then on to eastern and southern Africa. The dates are debated, but the first moves are often placed somewhere between about 3000 and 1500 BCE.

The early Bantu speakers lived in villages, made pottery, fished, and grew yams and oil palms. Iron working and cereal crops came later, along the way. The words their languages share for these things are one of the main clues to how the spread happened. The later map label Bantu peoples covers their descendants from 800 to 1500. The map's shape for 3000 and 2000 BCE stretches far wider than the homeland itself, so read it as a rough marker.
sum: This map label marks the early speakers of Bantu languages in west central Africa, shown in 3000 and 2000 BCE, before their descendants spread across most of the southern half of the continent.
